title: Why no intoxicants
hookLine: a clear mind is kept for remembrance

lines: A TRAY OF DRINKS, A THIRD TIME.
cards: A wedding reception, late. The music is loud, the tables crowded, and a tray of drinks comes around for the third time. One guest in a turban smiles, shakes his head, and asks for another glass of lime soda.
Nobody makes a fuss. His cousin says it the way you'd mention someone's shoe size: he's amritdhari, he doesn't drink. That's how the rule often gets met: a no.
But a rule seen only from the outside can look like a wall. What is this one protecting?

teach.h: THE CODE: NO ALCOHOL, NO TOBACCO.
teach.b: The code is plain. The Sikh Rehat Maryada tells a Sikh not to take alcohol, tobacco or other intoxicants, and tobacco is named again among the four things the initiated must never do, which you met early on this path.
The reason sits in the Guru Granth Sahib.

In a short verse by Guru Amar Das on Ang 554, a person pours a drink, it goes down, and, in paraphrase, understanding leaves, confusion comes in, and the drinker can no longer tell what is his own from what belongs to someone else.
Then the verse turns: don't drink this false drink if you can help it, and look for a different one. The Gurus don't only say no to one kind of drink; they talk about another.

teach.h: ANG 360: A WINE OF THE NAME.
teach.b: In a hymn by Guru Nanak on Ang 360, a distillery becomes a picture of the spiritual life: make wisdom the raw sugar, meditation the flowers, good deeds the bark, and the result is a wine of the Name.
Some readers call this the other intoxication, being soaked through with the remembrance of God. Now the wedding makes sense.

teach.h: A CLEAR MIND, KEPT FOR REMEMBRANCE.
teach.b: A clear mind is kept for remembrance: the morning prayers, the Name repeated, the eyes open to God in other people. Anything that clouds the mind clouds that. So the no isn't only a no.
It's a yes to staying awake. And it's no judgment on the table, either. The rule is about what a Sikh keeps clear in themselves, not about who else is holding a glass.

how: Sikhs who keep the Rehat Maryada abstain from alcohol, tobacco and other intoxicants, and amritdhari Sikhs are told at initiation never to use tobacco.

o: allowed if they're taken only at celebrations
only tobacco is barred; drink is left to choice
barred so the mind stays clear for remembering God

games.q: inside today's reason: tap the pairs.
p: no alcohol, tobacco or other intoxicants
a wine made of wisdom and good deeds

s: the Gurus only say no to drink and offer nothing in its place
Guru Nanak's hymn on Ang 360 pictures a different wine: the Name, made from wisdom, meditation and good deeds.
the code names tobacco among the things the initiated must never do
tobacco is named in the code's general rule and again for those who have taken amrit.
the rule is about judging the people around you
it's about what a Sikh keeps clear in themselves, not about who else is holding a glass.

games.q: in Guru Amar Das's verse, the drink goes down and the mind clouds. what does the verse do next?
o: it turns toward a different drink: the Name.
it lists a punishment for drinkers.
games.why: the verse turns: don't drink the false drink, look for another. the Gurus answer one intoxication with another, the remembrance of God.

practice: If a glass of water is close by, hold it up and notice how the light comes through, how you can see straight through it to the other side.
Then set it down and let the breath come and go, noticing how clear your own mind is right now, cloudy in places, bright in others, no grading. If you pray, let the word Waheguru ride on the breath.

wordCard.voice: Why no intoxicants. The code forbids alcohol, tobacco and other intoxicants, and the Gurus give the reason: the mind is kept clear for remembrance, and the only intoxication worth having is the Name. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: intoxication. the Gurus use the picture both ways: the drink that clouds, and the 'intoxication' of the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: clear mind. One drink refused, and another, the Name, offered. See you tomorrow.
